AMERICAN MODERNISM
1900-1945

units.label: page 2
units.text:
BETWEEN WORLD WARS
▪ Many historians have described the 
period between the two World Wars 
as a “traumatic coming of age.”
▪ In a post-Industrial Revolution era, 
America moved from an agrarian 
nation to an urban nation.
▪ The lives of these Americans were 
radically different from those of their 
parents.

units.label: page 3
units.text:
ROOTS OF 
MODERNISM
▪ Influenced by Walt 
Whitman’s free verse
▪ Prose poetry of British 
writer Oscar Wilde
▪ Emily Dickinson’s 
compression
▪ English Symbolist 
writers, especially 
Arthur Symons

units.label: page 4
units.text:
MODERNIST WRITERS
▪ Lost Generation Writers such as Ernest 
Hemingway, F. Scott Fitzgerald, William 
Faulkner, John Steinbeck, Gertrude 
Stein, T. S. Eliot, E. E. Cummings, Robert 
Frost
▪ Harlem Renaissance writers such as 
Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, 
James Weldon Johnson, Countee Cullen, 
Jean Toomer, Richard Wright

units.label: page 5
units.text:
CHARACTERISTICS
Modernist literature, which emerged in 
the late 19th and early 20th centuries, is 
characterized by:
• a rejection of traditional forms and 
conventions
• experimentation with narrative 
structure and style
• a focus on subjective experiences
• Fragmentation
• non-linear storytelling
• an emphasis on individualism

units.label: page 6
units.text:
THEMES
▪ Breakdown of social norms and cultural 
sureties
▪ Alienation of the individual
▪ Valorization of the despairing individual in 
the force of an unmanageable future 
▪ Product of the metropolis, of cities and 
urbanscapes

units.label: page 7
units.text:
THEME OF ALIENATION
▪ Sense of alienation in literature:
▪ The character belongs to a “lost 
generation” (Gertrude Stein)
▪ The character suffers from a 
“dissociation of sensibility”—
separation of thought from feeling 
(T. S. Eliot)
▪ The character has “a Dream 
deferred” (Langston Hughes).

units.label: page 8
units.text:
VALORIZATION OF THE INDIVIDUAL
▪ Characters are heroic in the face of a 
future they can’t control.
▪ Demonstrates the uncertainty felt by 
individuals living in this era.
▪ Examples include Jay Gatsby in The 
Great Gatsby, Lt. Henry in A Farewell to 
Arms

units.label: page 9
units.text:
SOCIAL/CULTURAL NORMS
▪ Women were given the right to vote in 1920.
▪ Hemlines raised; Margaret Sanger 
introduces the idea of birth control.
▪ Karl Marx’s ideas flourish; the Bolshevik 
Revolution overthrows Russia’s czarist 
government and establishes the Soviet 
Union.
▪ Writers begin to explore these new ideas.

units.label: page 10
units.text:
URBANSCAPES
▪ Life in the city differs 
from life on the farm; 
writers began to explore 
city life.
▪ Conflicts begin to center 
on society.

In Our Time is the title of 
Ernest Hemingway's first 
collection of short stories, 
published in 1925 by Boni & 
Liveright, New York.
Themes include alienation, loss, 
grief, and separation.
Considered one of Hemingway's 
early masterpieces.

units.label: page 16
units.text:
The story's protagonist is Harold 
Krebs, a young man who is unhappy 
after he returns home from serving in 
World War I.
The story begins with a very brief 
background of Krebs' life. Before the 
war, he attended a Methodist college 
in Kansas where he was part of a 
fraternity. In 1917, Krebs enlisted in 
the Marines and did not return to the 
United States from Germany until 
1919.
"Soldier's Home"

units.label: page 19
units.text:
Soldier’s Home: Major Themes
Theme Example from the Text Explanation of how this 
example shows the theme
Alienation/Isolation When he tries to talk about it, the people at 
home don’t listen to his stories about the war; 
Krebs has to lie, which makes him feel sick
This shows that Krebs has no one he can 
connect with in his home town, which makes 
him feel alienated from the people there.
War/Trauma The author writes about Krebs, “He did not 
want any consequences ever again”.
Clearly, the trauma that Krebs experienced in 
the war was so severe that any 
inconvenience in normal life feels like too 
much. After seeing so much death, he cannot 
readjust to normal life.
Loss/Grief When Krebs’ mother talks about God with 
him, Krebs’ says he “is not a part of God’s 
kingdom” and that he isn’t able to pray. 
This shows the loss of Krebs’ belief in God as 
he is not disillusioned with religion and belief. 
Clearly the way has shaken his faith.
Arrested Development When Krebs’ little sister asks if he can be her 
boyfriend, he says “sure” and plays along 
with his her childish behavior.
By this, the author shows that Krebs is stuck 
in an earlier stage of development, as he is 
too old be entertaining his sister’s childish 
games.

▪ Born in St. Paul Minnesota
▪ Upper-middle-class family
▪ Attended private school
▪ First published work when he was 15: a 
detective story in the school newspaper
▪ Attended Princeton University
▪ Focused on writing, which affected his marks 
and dropped out of uni

▪ During WWI, not deployed
▪ Wrote his greatest work during in the 1920’s
▪ Known as the “Roaring Twenties or the

units.label: page 21
units.text:
▪ Novels:
▪ This Side of Paradise (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1920)
▪ Greatest commercial success
▪ examines the lives and morality of post–World War I youth. Its protagonist, Amory Blaine, is an attractive 
Princeton University student who dabbles in literature. Theme of love warped by greed and status seeking.
▪ The Beautiful and Damned (New York: Scribners, 1922)
▪ New York café society and the American Eastern elite during the Jazz Age before and after WWI. Probably 
based on Fitzgerald's relationship and marriage with his wife Zelda Fitzgerald.
▪ The Great Gatsby (New York: Scribners, 1925)
▪ Literary masterpiece, not popular until after death
▪ The Great Gatsby explores themes of decadence, idealism, resistance to change, social upheaval, and excess, 
creating a portrait of the Jazz Age or the Roaring Twenties that has been described as a cautionary tale 
regarding the American Dream.
▪ Tender Is the Night (New York: Scribners, 1934)

Narrator and Main Characters 
(write down 
the first 3 points here)
▪ Nick Carraway – (unreliable) narrator and character in the novel
▪ Jay Gatsby – the elusive and enigmatic eponymous protagonist
▪ Daisy and Tom Buchanan – very wealthy married couple. Daisy is 
Nick’s cousin and Gatsby is in love with her. 
▪ Jordan Baker – a friend of the Buchanans, beautiful, cynical, young 
professional golfer – a sporting celebrity 
▪ George Wilson – runs a garage in an area called the Valley of the 
Ashes on the way to New York
▪ Myrtle Wilson – George’s wife and Tom Buchanan’s mistress

units.label: page 24
units.text:
Setting (will be on Moodle)
▪ The setting of the story is New York City and on Long Island, in 
two areas known as "West Egg" and "East Egg" —in real 
life, Great Neck and Port Washington peninsulas on Long 
Island.
▪ The main events of the novel take place in the summer of 
1922, in the period now known as the Jazz Age, just after the 
First World War and before the Great Depression of the 1930s. 
▪ However, there are flashbacks to Gatsby’s past and the time 
when he first met Daisy.

units.label: page 25
units.text:
Synopsis (Will be on Moodle)
▪ Set on Long Island and New York City, The Great Gatsby is narrated by 29-year-old 
Midwesterner Nick Carraway – also a character in the story, who comes to New York 
in 1922 to work in the bond business. 
▪ He rents a cheap bungalow next door to a mysterious man called Jay Gatsby who lives 
in a mock French mansion, and who throws extravagant parties every Saturday night. 
▪ Nick reconnects with his cousin, a Southern debutante named Daisy, the wife of Nick's 
racist Yale classmate, the staggeringly wealthy ex -football star Tom Buchanan.
▪ Nick meets Jordan Baker, friend of the Buchanans, the beautiful professional golfer.
▪ He learns that Tom has a mistress, Myrtle Wilson, wife of a garage mechanic in Valley 
of the Ashes, a grey industrial dumping ground on the way to New York.

units.label: page 26
units.text:
Synopsis (Will be on Moodle)
▪ Eventually Nick is invited to one of Gatsby’s famous parties and discovers that no 
one there actually knows who Gatsby is. 
▪ However, he meets Gatsby and they become friendly. However, Nick realises 
that Gatsby lies about his past and he remains a mystery for Nick (and the 
reader)
▪ Nick discovers that Gatsby is in love with Daisy whom he met and fell in love with 
during the war when he was in uniform, and therefore unidentifiable as poor and 
working class, which he was.  
▪ Gatsby's obsession with Daisy, whom he loved as a young Army officer stationed 
in Louisville right before World War I, fuels this tale of longing and loss, of 
dreams and disillusion.

units.label: page 27
units.text:
But what is the novel actually about? (take 
these notes!)
▪ The American Dream – about acquiring wealth and status in society; – Gatsby represents 
America itself
▪ Greed and hypocrisy
▪ Fitzgerald decouples wealth and greatness. In this novel wealth is associated with 
corruption and amorality.
▪ Truth
▪ Class divisions
▪ A reflection on the hollowness of a life of leisure
▪ Gatsby is obsessed with controlling time: he wants to create a beautiful future by restoring 
the past. This is what leads Gatsby to say his most famous line "Can't change the past? Why, 
of course you can."

units.label: page 28
units.text:
Symbolism (take note of this)
▪ The green light at the end of Daisy’s dock across 
the bay represents hope and the American 
Dream to Jay Gatsby
“If it wasn’t for the mist we could see your home 
across the bay,” said Gatsby. “You always have a 
green light that burns all night at the end of your 
dock.”
“And as I sat there brooding on the old, unknown 
world, I thought of Gatsby’s wonder when he first 
picked out the green light at the end of Daisy’s dock.”

units.text:
▪ Born in Mississippi
▪ Father was the treasurer of the family railway company
▪ Hoped to inherit the company, but didn’t
▪ Influenced mainly by mother, maternal grandmother
▪ Raised mostly by a black woman hired to care for the 
children
▪ Mother’s family was more academic/artistic and 
encouraged reading
▪ Avid reader and decent student, also heard lots of stories 
from older people in his community
▪ Civil War stories, slavery, the Ku Klux Klan, and the 
Falkner family, including Faulkner's great -grandfather, a 
successful businessman, writer, and Civil War hero called 
"Old Colonel"
▪ Much of this can be seen in his work

units.label: page 31
units.text:
▪ The Sound and the Fury (Jonathan Cape & Harrison Smith, 1929)
▪ Title from Macbeth scene 5, act 5
▪ stream of consciousness; 4 parts each narrated by different family member
▪ Compson family, former Southern aristocrats who are struggling to deal with the dissolution of their family and its reputation
▪ As I Lay Dying (Jonathan Cape & Harrison Smith, 1930)
▪ Title from Book XI of Homer's The Odyssey
▪ stream of consciousness writing technique, 15 different narrators over 59 chapters
▪ death of Addie Bundren and her poor, rural family's quest and motivations – noble or selfish – to honor her wish to be buried in  
her hometown of Jefferson, Mississippi
▪ Absalom, Absalom! (Random House, 1936)
▪ Title from the biblical story of Absalom, a son of David who rebelled against his father
▪ rise and fall of Thomas Sutpen
▪ entirely in flashbacks narrated mostly by Quentin Compson to his roommate (Shreve)
▪ Rosa Coldfield, and Quentin's father and grandfather, are also included and re -interpreted by Shreve and Quentin, with the total  
events of the story unfolding in nonchronological order and often with conflicting information.

units.label: page 32
units.text:
As I Lay Dying (1930)
▪ As a leader of the Modernist Movement, 
Faulkner’s primary accomplishment is 
his use of experimental narration.
▪ As I Lay Dying is told by 15 separate 
narrators, each telling his or her own 
version of the events, sometimes 
supporting and sometimes contradicting 
each other.
▪ Written in a stream of consciousness 
style
